newsitem.title: philippines: Seoul said to reassure U.S. on N. Korea deal.
newsitem.headline: Seoul said to reassure U.S. on N. Korea deal.

text.p: The United States expressed confidence on Friday that a multi-billion dollar landmark nuclear agreement with North Korea would go ahead after reassurances South Korea remains committed to the deal.
Officials said they still believed Seoul required some sort of "gesture" by Pyongyang to "atone for the sins" of its submarine incursion into the South last September.
But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters he expected that gesture would be forthcoming.
Meeting U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha "said he agreed it was important to preserve the agreed framework," Burns said.
He referred to the 1994 accord with Washington under which Pyongyang froze its nuclear programme in return for two nuclear power reactors and alternative energy suppies.
Once expected to cost $4.5 billion, Burns said the South Korean minister now uses the figure $6 billion for the project.
Yoo also said "it was important that KEDO meet its commitments as part of the agreed framework. The secretary said he was very reassured to hear that," Burns said.
KEDO, the Korean Energy Development Organisation, was formed by the United States, South Korea and Japan to underwrite and manage the U.S.-North Korean nuclear agreement.
The Christopher-Yoo talks laid the ground for a meeting on Sunday between U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.
Much of the discussion dealt with whether Europeans would be permitted to join KEDO after making a large financial contribution, Burns said.

Tense relations between the two Koreas have worsened since a North Korean submarine landed 26 agents on a South Korean beach in September. Twenty-four of them were shot dead, one was captured alive and another is still at large.
The North insists the incident was an accident and demands the return of the bodies and the captured agent.

South Korea says it will suspend all assistance to the North, including financing for nuclear plants, until it "clearly apologises" for the submarine incident and guarantees such an incident will not be repeated.
Seoul recently delayed sending technicians to do site work preparation for the reactors in the North. Pyongyang responded by threatening to end its nuclear freeze.

U.S. officials are trying to bring the two sides back together. Burns gave no reason for expecting North Korea to make a sufficient "gesture" to the South. But officials have met weekly in New York with North Korean counterparts.
A U.S. congressman who often serves as an unofficial White House envoy, Representative Bill Richardson, visits North Korea next week.
